title: Do We Still Need Reinforcement Learning When We Can Read the World Model?
authors: Mingchao Zhang, Miduo Cui, Kangze He, Yuanjun Li, Dapeng Li, Ce Zhang
abstract: Reinforcement learning has achieved remarkable success in sequential decision-making, but learning effective policies often requires substantial interaction experience. Model-based reinforcement learning alleviates this dependence by leveraging world models, which are typically used to support planning or policy optimization. In this paper, we investigate an alternative paradigm in which autonomous LLM-based coding agents directly synthesize control policies by reasoning over readable world models. By examining environment source code, these agents translate environmental knowledge into executable decision rules and iteratively refine their policies using online feedback or offline data, without task-specific RL training. Experiments across diverse decision-making benchmarks show that synthesized policies match or outperform conventional RL methods while requiring substantially less experience. Further analyses reveal interpretable decision rules and how they evolve through feedback-driven refinement. Comparisons with policies generated without source code access and experiments under challenging conditions further demonstrate the benefits of readable world models. These findings suggest that direct policy synthesis can reduce reliance on trial and error, challenging the necessity of task-specific RL training.

infographic.key_insight: LLM coding agents can synthesize effective control policies directly from readable environment source code, reducing reliance on task-specific reinforcement learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For systems with accessible environment code, direct policy synthesis could reduce interaction costs while producing interpretable, executable decision rules.
method: Read environment source code to understand dynamics and constraints.
Translate this knowledge into executable control policies.
Refine policies using online feedback or offline data, without task-specific RL training.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across diverse decision-making benchmarks, synthesized policies matched or outperformed conventional RL methods with substantially less experience; comparisons also examined source-code access and challenging conditions.
infographic.watch_item: Applicability to systems without readable, faithful environment source code remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Do We Still Need Reinforcement Learning When We Can Read the World Model?

title: REE: A Scientific Research Entrance Exam for AI Agents
authors: Zeqi Zhou, Minghao Liu, Jiarui Liu, Qingcheng Zeng, Rui Yang, Tianyu Liu
abstract: Autonomous research agents are emerging as a promising approach to scientific problem-solving across disciplines, owing to their growing ability to improve a solution through repeated experiments. Evaluating this ability requires benchmarks that pose open-ended research problems and measure improvements over established scientific methods. We introduce REE (Research Entrance Exam), a benchmark that tests AI agents on scientific research. It consists of 100 open-ended research problems spanning five broad scientific areas and 23 domains. To ensure high quality, every problem is drawn from active research in its field and individually reviewed by domain experts. Each problem is posed as a task of iterative improvement: an agent has up to 12 hours to improve a working starter solution, and REE scores the result on a common scale against an established expert solution evaluated under comparable conditions. By this measure, two of the four frontier agents we evaluate, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, outperform the expert solutions on 86% and 81% of problems, across all five scientific areas. Their runs also show how they do so: both agents surpass the expert solutions within the first two hours on average, and their best solutions mostly tailor or combine established methods of the field. REE thus provides a unified framework for evaluating autonomous scientific research, capturing both improvements over established methods and the research processes behind them.

infographic.key_insight: REE benchmarks autonomous scientific research through iterative improvement, with two evaluated agents outperforming expert solutions on more than 80% of problems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: REE offers a shared framework for evaluating whether research agents can improve working scientific solutions under a fixed time budget.
method: Use 100 expert-reviewed, open-ended problems across five scientific areas and 23 domains.
Give agents up to 12 hours to iteratively improve a working starter solution.
Score improvements against established expert solutions evaluated under comparable conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among four frontier agents evaluated, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol beat expert solutions on 86% and 81% of problems, respectively, surpassing them within two hours on average.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark gains should not be equated with novel discoveries: the best solutions mostly tailored or combined established methods.
infographic.paper_title: REE: A Scientific Research Entrance Exam for AI Agents

title: Adaptive Reliability Reserves for Residential Battery Fleets
authors: Maruthi Vemula, Neeraj Praneeth Gajula
abstract: In a Houston 2024 replay, replacing a fixed 20 percent battery reserve with a county-risk threshold raises observed five-hour backup coverage from 75.0 percent to 86.5 percent and adds USD 10.2 in modeled annualized margin per home (paired 95 percent interval: USD +1.7 to USD +21.7). The paired coverage-gain interval includes zero. This is a conditional simulation result, not measured company reliability. Residential batteries face this tradeoff because market discharge consumes energy also needed for household outages. We release HomeFleet-ERCOT, combining observed prices and county outages with identified simulated homes and causal controller inputs. We compare independent-home optimization with 21 proximal policy optimization (PPO) training runs; ten promise-cost candidates span 31.1 percent-96.3 percent backup coverage. Of these, 10 have lower modeled margin than fixed 20 percent, and 3 also have lower coverage. Chronological, geographic, fleet, and storm tests examine transfer. An alert charging override has a conditional energy-and-power sufficiency guarantee, but only 19.5 percent of 41 county mass-outage episodes provide enough continuous warning for every battery preset. Synthetic tests include short, missed, and false warnings, load uplift, capacity loss, and dropout. A static AC audit retains existing feeder violations; aging comparisons expose model sensitivity. The released benchmark, controllers, and checkpoints provide a reproducible basis for comparing these tradeoffs. This work supports the design of residential battery programs that assess market value and household backup service together.

infographic.key_insight: In a Houston 2024 simulation replay, a county-risk reserve policy increased observed five-hour backup coverage from 75.0% to 86.5% and modeled annualized margin by USD 10.2 per home versus a fixed 20% reserve.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Risk-adaptive battery reserves could help residential fleets balance market revenue with household backup service.
method: Release HomeFleet-ERCOT, pairing observed prices and county outages with identified simulated homes and causal controller inputs.
Compare independent-home optimization with 21 proximal policy optimization (PPO) training runs.
Evaluate transfer across time, geography, fleets, and storms, plus synthetic warning failures and battery degradation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paired 95% interval for annualized margin gain was USD +1.7 to +21.7 per home, while the coverage-gain interval included zero; only 19.5% of 41 county mass-outage episodes provided enough continuous warning for every battery preset.
infographic.watch_item: Results are conditional simulations, not measured company reliability; alert-based charging guarantees depend on sufficient warning, energy, and power.
infographic.paper_title: Adaptive Reliability Reserves for Residential Battery Fleets

title: One Model, Many Modes: Evolving System Prompt Ensembles for Creative Generation
authors: Daiwei Chen, Anda He, Binwei Yao, Junjie Hu, Ramya Korlakai Vinayak
abstract: Preference-aligned LLMs can exhibit mode collapse, concentrating their output distributions around a narrow set of high-reward responses. This limits creative generation, which requires quality, novelty, and diversity. Existing test-time methods often emphasize diversity, giving less attention to whether individual responses are both high-quality and novel. This distinction matters in practical use, where users may seek a single compelling, original response. We formalize creative generation as a multi-objective distributional optimization problem and introduce SEPO, a training-free framework for System Prompt Ensemble Optimization. The framework combines prompt evolution with greedy max-min selection to identify behaviorally distinct system prompts under a quality constraint, then uniformly samples one prompt per response at inference time. Across four creative generation tasks with increasing quality requirements and three open-weight models, SEPO ranks first in 8 of 12 settings on the harmonic mean of quality, diversity, and novelty, while no baseline leads in more than two. On average, it raises LLM-judged diversity from 1.92 to 3.43 and novelty from 1.00 to 3.34 over base sampling (1-5 scale), with quality decreasing from 3.72 to 3.30. We further show that expanding the optimized ensemble increases separation among prompt-conditioned response distributions. These results support system prompt ensemble optimization as a promising approach to improving LLM creativity at inference time.

infographic.key_insight: SEPO improves creative generation by evolving diverse system prompts and sampling among them, trading some response quality for higher novelty and diversity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can diversify outputs from a single LLM at inference time without retraining, using an optimized ensemble of system prompts.
method: Evolve candidate system prompts to elicit distinct response behaviors.
Use greedy max-min selection to build a diverse ensemble under a quality constraint.
Uniformly sample one ensemble prompt per generated response.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four tasks and three open-weight models, SEPO led 8 of 12 settings on the harmonic mean of quality, diversity, and novelty; average LLM-judged diversity rose from 1.92 to 3.43 and novelty from 1.00 to 3.34 on a 1–5 scale.
infographic.watch_item: Average quality fell from 3.72 to 3.30, so deployments should validate the creativity–quality trade-off against task-specific requirements.
infographic.paper_title: One Model, Many Modes: Evolving System Prompt Ensembles for Creative Generation

title: Provably Efficient Concave Utility Reinforcement Learning with Linear Function Approximation
authors: Max Qiushi Lin, Ahmed Magd, Sharan Vaswani
abstract: Concave utility reinforcement learning (CURL) unifies a diverse range of problems, including standard reinforcement learning (RL), imitation learning, and maximum entropy exploration. Unlike standard RL, CURL generally requires estimating high-dimensional state-action occupancy measures. Consequently, existing methods for CURL either sidestep the exploration problem, are restricted to the tabular setting, or lack computationally efficient policy optimization. To address this, we study CURL in finite-horizon episodic bilinear MDPs, where the transition model admits a low-dimensional representation in known feature spaces. We use the bilinear structure to efficiently estimate occupancy measures via low-dimensional feature expectations, and propose a model-based optimistic concave utility policy optimization (OCUPO) framework. We first instantiate OCUPO in the on-policy setting, where each iteration uses independent trajectories to estimate the concave utility policy gradient, and prove an $\widetilde{O}(ε^{-4})$ sample complexity. To improve sample efficiency, we then instantiate OCUPO in the off-policy setting. We propose a novel backward feature regression subroutine that reuses trajectories collected by past policies to estimate the occupancy measure of the current policy. Under suitable technical assumptions on the policy class (satisfied, e.g., by log-linear policies with sufficiently expressive features), we prove that the resulting algorithm achieves an $\widetilde{O}(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity, up to a controllable projection error. We further extend our framework to linear MDPs and show that the resulting off-policy algorithm retains the same sample complexity. In these settings, the dependence on $ε$ matches that for standard RL with linear function approximation. Moreover, our algorithms do not rely on the integral oracle required by prior work.

infographic.key_insight: Low-dimensional feature expectations enable computationally efficient concave utility reinforcement learning, with off-policy sample complexity matching standard RL’s dependence on target accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports reward maximization, imitation learning, and maximum-entropy exploration without directly estimating high-dimensional state-action occupancy measures.
method: Exploit known feature spaces in finite-horizon bilinear MDPs to estimate occupancy measures.
Use model-based optimistic concave utility policy optimization (OCUPO).
Reuse past trajectories through backward feature regression, with an extension to linear MDPs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical sample-complexity guarantees of Õ(ε⁻⁴) on-policy and Õ(ε⁻²) off-policy, up to controllable projection error; it reports no empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The off-policy guarantee requires suitable policy-class assumptions, while practical accuracy depends on controlling projection error.
infographic.paper_title: Provably Efficient Concave Utility Reinforcement Learning with Linear Function Approximation

title: Make the Adversary Spend More: Stateful Deception as a Cost-Exchange Primitive for AI-Era Cyber Defense
authors: Alessandro Cantelli-Forti, Isabella Marasco, Hosam Alamleh, Giada Boschi, Michele Colajanni
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming the economics of intrusion by reducing the attacker's cost to scan and adapt, while tempting defenders into unbounded compute. We argue that cyber deception should be judged by the cost exchange it imposes, not by realism or detection, and that the primitive making that exchange favorable is adversary-specific persistent state. Rather than a honeypot that resets or merges sessions, each recognized adversary re-enters the world it believes it has compromised, kept coherent with its own past actions and isolated from every other adversary, while the language model acts only as a constrained renderer of explicit state, never as its store. We formalize the trade-off as a Deception Exchange Rate (DER), relating mission-weighted adversary effort burned to defender resources spent, and instantiate it in an SSH honeypot pairing Cowrie with a local LLM. In this paper, we focus on the defender-side evaluation of that exchange, while specifying, but not yet measuring, per-adversary state and the adversary side of the DER. Across five open-weight models, deterministic-layer and prompt optimizations cut per-session defender cost by around 63% against a naive all-LLM decoy.

infographic.key_insight: Stateful deception aims to make attackers spend more than defenders by preserving a coherent, isolated decoy world for each recognized adversary.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Explicit state management and deterministic responses can limit LLM compute costs while supporting persistent cyber-deception environments.
method: Define a Deception Exchange Rate comparing mission-weighted adversary effort with defender resource spending.
Pair a Cowrie SSH honeypot with a local LLM constrained to render explicit state rather than store it.
Optimize deterministic handling and prompts to reduce reliance on LLM generation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five open-weight models, deterministic-layer and prompt optimizations reduced per-session defender cost by around 63% versus a naive all-LLM decoy.
infographic.watch_item: Per-adversary state and attacker-side effort are specified but not yet measured, so a favorable end-to-end cost exchange remains unverified.
infographic.paper_title: Make the Adversary Spend More: Stateful Deception as a Cost-Exchange Primitive for AI-Era Cyber Defense

title: Hierarchical Graph Metanetworks
authors: Ioannis Kalogeropoulos, Giorgos Bouritsas, Yannis Panagakis
abstract: The emerging field of weight space learning has demonstrated the potential to enable metanetworks, i.e. models that process neural network (NN) data, to support several steps of the machine learning lifecycle, from model optimisation to evaluation and adaptation. However, this potential has yet to materialise beyond small-scale MLPs or CNNs: most current models, including message-passing based graph metanetworks (GMNs), operate exclusively at the finest level of granularity, processing every neuron and weight of the input model. Their cost therefore scales with the number of parameters. Yet NNs are inherently organised hierarchically, with neurons forming layers and layers forming blocks and modules. Additionally, several of their properties, such as Lipschitz upper bounds and generalisation measures, are compositions of layer- and block-level quantities. To incorporate this inductive bias, we introduce Hierarchical Graph Metanetworks (H-GMNs), which leverage the input architecture's hierarchy to coarsen and refine the graph using permutation-symmetry-preserving pooling and un-pooling layers. Further, we extend H-GMNs to Transformers by introducing a graph construction that preserves permutation symmetries and enables multi-level pooling. Our evaluation includes new ResNet-18, ViT and varying ViT model zoos of up to 86M parameters, on tasks spanning model evaluation (an analytic Lipschitz bound proxy, generalisation and robustness prediction), testing (backdoor detection) and editing (pruning). Experimental results show that, compared to non-equivariant alternatives and flat GMNs, H-GMNs are markedly more sample-efficient, and their cost remains nearly constant as metanetwork depth grows, allowing deeper and more expressive processing where flat GMNs run out of memory, without compromising accuracy, which in certain cases considerably improves.

infographic.key_insight: Hierarchical Graph Metanetworks exploit neural-network hierarchy to process weight-space graphs more efficiently than flat graph metanetworks while preserving permutation symmetries.
infographic.engineering_relevance: H-GMNs enable deeper metanetworks for evaluating, testing and editing large neural networks without the memory growth of flat graph processing.
method: Represent neural networks as graphs organised into neuron, layer and block levels.
Coarsen and refine graphs using permutation-symmetry-preserving pooling and unpooling.
Extend hierarchical processing to Transformers with a symmetry-preserving graph construction.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations on ResNet-18 and ViT model zoos with models up to 86M parameters cover Lipschitz-bound proxy, generalisation and robustness prediction, backdoor detection and pruning, reporting improved sample efficiency and nearly constant cost as metanetwork depth grows.
infographic.watch_item: Nearly constant cost is reported with increasing metanetwork depth, not increasing input-model size; architecture-specific graph construction remains an implementation consideration.
infographic.paper_title: Hierarchical Graph Metanetworks

title: Learning to Be Truncated: Preparing LLM Checkpoints for SVD Compression
authors: Chenyue Fang, Danila Mishin, Babak Falsafi
abstract: Compression based on singular value decomposition (SVD) often requires subsequent fine-tuning or weight correction to mitigate performance degradation. Budget-specific optimization must be repeated for different compression ratios. We introduce LLift, which prepares a pretrained model for SVD compression across ratios without further fine-tuning. LLift fine-tunes a low-rank approximation at a single ratio using the original model as a teacher. We merge the learned updates into the original weights while preserving the complementary components excluded from the training forward pass. We apply SVD to the prepared model's target matrices and reuse the decompositions at different truncation ranks. On LLaMA-7B, we demonstrate accuracy gains across three compression ratios using a single prepared model. The gains extend across model families, model sizes, and SVD compression operators. We analyze gradients and an early training update to provide local evidence that updates learned at one ratio can benefit compression at other ratios. These results show that LLift can improve compression across deployment budgets without fine-tuning each compressed model separately.

infographic.key_insight: LLift prepares one pretrained LLM checkpoint for SVD compression at multiple ratios without separately fine-tuning each compressed model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A single preparation step and reusable SVD decompositions can simplify deployment across different model-compression budgets.
method: Fine-tune a low-rank approximation at one compression ratio using the original model as teacher.
Merge learned updates into the original weights while preserving components excluded from the training forward pass.
Decompose the prepared target matrices once and reuse their SVDs at different truncation ranks.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports accuracy gains on LLaMA-7B at three compression ratios, with gains also observed across model families, sizes, and SVD compression operators.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify accuracy gains or preparation costs, so deployment benefits require workload-specific validation.
infographic.paper_title: Learning to Be Truncated: Preparing LLM Checkpoints for SVD Compression

title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents
authors: Han Huang, Yuchen Yan, Xingyu Wu, Yijun Li, Chao Deng, Jie Liu
abstract: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.

infographic.key_insight: DRBench Pro evaluates deep research reports by structured knowledge coverage, distinguishing breadth across research directions from depth along related knowledge chains.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Agent developers can use separate breadth and depth scores to diagnose coverage gaps that aggregate report-quality ratings may obscure.
method: Build local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and sample subgraphs to generate research queries.
Create evidence-grounded rubrics tied to tree relations; agents receive only the query.
Measure breadth and depth, then combine them using their geometric mean.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 144 cases in 24 domains with 44,102 rubrics, 16 agents were evaluated; the best achieved 57.04% overall coverage, with close human agreement on rubric judgments and stable rankings across tested metric configurations.
infographic.watch_item: Wikipedia-derived knowledge trees may not capture specialized, emerging, or non-encyclopedic research knowledge.
infographic.paper_title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents

title: Transferring Architecture as an Optimization Prior
authors: Vighnesh Subramaniam, Boris Katz, Brian Cheung
abstract: Initialization determines the optimization "fate" of a model, going far beyond just setting the scale of its weights. It establishes a fundamental initial geometry over the input data, dictating certain aspects such as which examples are considered close and which representations gradient descent will naturally refine first. In this paper, we view the initial geometry of a network as an optimization prior and ask whether a network can change its optimization prior by referencing a completely different architecture. To investigate this question, we use an initialization procedure where a target network is aligned to the representational geometry of a randomly initialized guide network before any downstream training occurs. Crucially, alignment to the guide network cannot transfer learned features, never receives gradients, and does not use labels. We demonstrate that this cross-architecture transfer of "fate" benefits the target network in two key domains: (1) instilling the optimization benefits of depth into shallow networks by aligning them to deeper networks, and (2) transferring representational granularity by using fine-resolution networks to shape the geometry of networks with coarser representations. In both cases, the alignment results in improved downstream performance of the target network. Ultimately, this demonstrates that a model's architectural destiny can be decoupled from its physical structure and explicitly modified at initialization.

infographic.key_insight: Aligning a target network’s initial representational geometry with a randomly initialized guide can transfer architectural optimization benefits without transferring learned features.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This initialization strategy could improve shallow or coarse-representation networks without changing their physical architecture.
method: Use a randomly initialized network with a different architecture as a fixed guide.
Align the target’s representational geometry to the guide before downstream training, without labels or gradients to the guide.
Train the aligned target on the downstream task.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved downstream performance when shallow networks are aligned to deeper guides and coarse-representation networks to fine-resolution guides, but provides no datasets or numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify alignment overhead or establish how reliably gains generalize across tasks and architecture pairs.
infographic.paper_title: Transferring Architecture as an Optimization Prior

title: Fewer Parameters, Longer Runtimes: The Wall-Clock Cost of Hybrid Quantum Physics-Informed Neural Networks
authors: Leyan Lyu, Shabnam Jabeen
abstract: While hybrid quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks (QCPINNs) are often described as efficient because they have fewer trainable parameters than classical PINNs, parameter count does not measure wall-clock cost. To examine this gap on a one-dimensional seawater temperature diffusion benchmark, with the quantum circuits simulated on a CPU, we time the four cumulative stages a PINN needs (the forward pass, the first- and second-order input gradients, and the PDE-loss parameter gradient) for a classical PINN, four hybrid configurations that differ in qubit count and circuit depth, and size-matched classical controls that share the hybrids' classical layers. We find that the hybrids are 14-56x slower than the classical PINN for the forward pass and 10-97x slower for the PDE-loss parameter gradient, and even against the size-matched controls, they remain 9-85x slower. Further, over the tested ranges, runtime increased approximately exponentially with qubit count, approximately linearly with circuit depth, and sub-linearly with batch size, while for the circuit-only forward pass, a second simulator backend was 10-165x slower under the same calling pattern. Although the hybrids have 38-44% fewer parameters than the classical PINN, this reduction comes from their smaller classical layers, as the quantum circuit accounts for at most 2.5% of each hybrid's parameters. Yet parameter count failed to predict runtime even among the classical networks, since the size-matched controls, despite having fewer parameters than the classical PINN, run slower than it. Our conclusion is that fewer parameters did not mean lower cost: every hybrid took at least ten times longer than the classical PINN at every stage, and the gap grew quickly with the number of qubits.

infographic.key_insight: Hybrid quantum PINNs used 38–44% fewer parameters but ran substantially slower than a classical PINN, showing that parameter count is not a reliable proxy for computational cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Benchmark wall-clock time across derivative and loss-gradient computations before choosing a quantum–classical architecture for physics-informed learning.
method: Evaluate a 1D seawater temperature diffusion benchmark with quantum circuits simulated on a CPU.
Compare a classical PINN, four hybrid configurations, and classical controls matched to the hybrids’ classical layers.
Time four cumulative stages: forward pass, first input gradient, second input gradient, and PDE-loss parameter gradient.
infographic.evidence_signal: Hybrids were 14–56× slower for forward passes and 10–97× slower for PDE-loss parameter gradients than the classical PINN; runtime increased approximately exponentially with qubit count over the tested range.
infographic.watch_item: Results concern a single benchmark with CPU-simulated circuits and should not be generalized directly to quantum hardware or other execution setups.
infographic.paper_title: Fewer Parameters, Longer Runtimes: The Wall-Clock Cost of Hybrid Quantum Physics-Informed Neural Networks

title: Find the Clue, Not the Scene: Rethinking Reasoning for Entity Recognition in Vision-Language Models
authors: Kyungmin Min, Soyeon Kim, Junseok Kim, Kyomin Jung
abstract: Answering a knowledge-based visual question requires first recognizing the entity in the image and then recalling knowledge about it. Thinking vision-language models (VLMs) reason for thousands of tokens before answering, yet it remains underexplored how well such thinking VLMs perform each of these two steps. We therefore analyze thinking VLMs on this task and make two key observations. (1) Recognition is the bottleneck, since 76.3% of errors across four models on ViQuAE stem from misrecognizing the entity, and 84.9% of these failures are resolved once the entity name is provided in the question. (2) Recognition is driven by entity-recall clues rather than by general descriptions of the image. An entity-recall clue is a distinctive visual detail that helps the model recall the entity, such as keys, a traditional attribute of Saint Peter. Based on these findings, we propose ClueRL, a reinforcement learning approach that extends Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with an advantage localized to the entity-recall clue in the thinking trace. Rather than injecting new entity knowledge, ClueRL changes how VLMs think: it leads them to attend more closely to visual details and spot these clues, helping them use the knowledge they already have. Consequently, it outperforms both GRPO and a perception-reward baseline on three entity recognition benchmarks. Moreover, this clue-seeking behavior generalizes beyond entity recognition, the only task used for training. Since recognition is the bottleneck, the gains carry over to knowledge-based visual question answering. They even extend to general multimodal reasoning, raising Qwen3.5-4B by 4.4 and 4.0 points on the ScienceQA and MMMU subsets of MMStar, respectively.

infographic.key_insight: Entity recognition—not knowledge recall—is the main bottleneck, and distinctive visual clues help VLMs identify entities better than general scene descriptions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Training VLMs to seek entity-specific visual clues can improve recognition and downstream reasoning without injecting new entity knowledge.
method: Identify entity-recall clues: distinctive visual details linked to an entity, such as Saint Peter’s keys.
Extend GRPO with an advantage localized to the entity-recall clue in the thinking trace.
Train on entity recognition to encourage clue-seeking behavior that transfers to other tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four models on ViQuAE, misrecognition caused 76.3% of errors; ClueRL outperformed GRPO and a perception-reward baseline on three recognition benchmarks and improved Qwen3.5-4B by 4.4 and 4.0 points on MMStar’s ScienceQA and MMMU subsets.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify how clue spans are identified or supervised, leaving the implementation cost of localized rewards unclear.
infographic.paper_title: Find the Clue, Not the Scene: Rethinking Reasoning for Entity Recognition in Vision-Language Models

title: DemoFoundry: Toward Scalable Photorealistic Robot Data with Coding Agents and Generative Rendering
authors: Ruixiang Wang, Xinyue Yao, Xuanning Zhou, Yueci Deng, Yongyi Su, Kui Jia
abstract: Scaling robot learning requires demonstrations that combine realistic visual observations with reliable action supervision. Simulation-based synthesis faces a substantial visual gap relative to real environments, while video-only generation struggles to maintain physically consistent interactions and provide aligned action labels. We present DemoFoundry, an automated framework that couples coding agents with generative rendering to synthesize photorealistic and physically grounded robot demonstrations. Coding agents both construct aligned real--proxy video pairs from existing robot episodes to train a video renderer and write executable interaction programs to generate new demonstrations. Given a scene reference and task instruction, an agent reconstructs task-relevant geometry and writes a control program without requiring target-task human demonstrations. Program execution in a physics simulator produces proxy videos with aligned robot states and actions. The video renderer translates these proxy videos into scene-consistent, photorealistic observations, reducing the need for detailed appearance modeling in each scene. Automated task-execution checks select successful trajectories for rendering and policy learning. Experiments show improved visual quality and action--video consistency. Policies trained on the generated demonstrations outperform raw-simulation training and approach the performance of training on an equal number of real demonstrations.

infographic.key_insight: DemoFoundry combines coding agents, physics simulation, and generative rendering to create photorealistic robot demonstrations with aligned action supervision.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework reduces reliance on target-task human demonstrations and detailed scene appearance modeling when generating robot-training data.
method: Coding agents construct aligned real–proxy video pairs to train a video renderer.
Given a scene reference and task instruction, agents reconstruct task-relevant geometry and write executable robot-control programs.
Simulation produces proxy videos and aligned states/actions; automated checks select successful trajectories for photorealistic rendering and policy learning.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved visual quality and action–video consistency, with generated-data policies outperforming raw-simulation training and approaching training on an equal number of real demonstrations.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment should verify that generative rendering preserves task-critical physical interactions and action alignment across new scenes.
infographic.paper_title: DemoFoundry: Toward Scalable Photorealistic Robot Data with Coding Agents and Generative Rendering

title: Repairing the Trustworthiness of Distilled Language Models
authors: Kumar Shubham, Devendra Vyas, Vidushi Agarwal, Jayin Khanna, Prathosh AP
abstract: Knowledge distillation enables the deployment of large language models through smaller student models, but the compression process can introduce regressions in trustworthiness even when downstream performance is preserved. Repairing such failures is challenging because the original distillation corpus is often unavailable, while direct preference optimization may alter capabilities inherited from the teacher. We propose a targeted repair framework based on the proximal Bregman response function (PBRF) that addresses both limitations. We estimate the curvature required for PBRF using a surrogate proxy dataset, removing dependence on the original transfer corpus, and extend the framework to preference-based supervision through an odds-ratio objective. This enables the use of preferred and dispreferred response pairs while constraining changes to the distilled model. Our results show that the proposed approach improves targeted trustworthiness behaviors for both pre-training and post-training models while largely preserving downstream performance, providing a practical alternative to re-distillation or unconstrained preference optimization. Our experiment results show that across different distilled models, the trustworthy regression can be improved by up to 8% with less than 1% decrement in perplexity.

infographic.key_insight: Targeted repair can improve trustworthiness in distilled language models while largely preserving capabilities inherited from the teacher.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a practical alternative to re-distillation when the original distillation corpus is unavailable.
method: Use a proximal Bregman response function (PBRF) to constrain changes during repair.
Estimate the required curvature using a surrogate proxy dataset.
Incorporate preferred and dispreferred response pairs through an odds-ratio objective.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across different distilled models in pre-training and post-training settings, the abstract reports trustworthiness improvements of up to 8% with less than 1% decrement in perplexity.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify proxy-dataset sensitivity or whether the reported perplexity decrement denotes improvement or degradation.
infographic.paper_title: Repairing the Trustworthiness of Distilled Language Models

title: Distractor-Robust Reinforcement Learning via Variational Bisimulation
authors: Benjamin Freed, Vivaan Singh, Dean Zadok, Roberto Calandra, Jeff Schneider, Howie Choset
abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) promises data efficiency and generalization, but typical reconstruction-based objectives encourage models to waste representational capacity on task-irrelevant distractors. We introduce VIBES (Variational Inference for Bisimulation-based Encoded States), a new objective that replaces pixel reconstruction with an adversarial term, which enforces that latent states suffice to predict both rewards and the next latent state. We show that this objective measures how far the encoder is from reward and dynamics sufficiency, and that whenever exact sufficiency is attainable, its global optima induce bisimulation relations on histories. Combined with a fixed-capacity latent bottleneck, this encourages latent states to retain task-relevant information while discarding irrelevant variation. Our method serves as a drop-in replacement for Dreamer's model-learning component, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Distracting Control Suite, and extends to visually complex manipulation in Realistic ManiSkill. Unlike prior approaches, it does not rely on image-specific augmentations and applies equally well to high-dimensional vector-state tasks, demonstrated on a 100-link swimmer robot. Finally, latent-space analyses (UMAP embeddings and nearest-neighbor probes) confirm that the learned representations are sensitive to task-relevant structure while invariant to distractors.

infographic.key_insight: VIBES replaces pixel reconstruction with a sufficiency-focused objective that helps reinforcement learning models retain task-relevant information while ignoring distractors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Designed as a drop-in replacement for Dreamer’s model-learning component, VIBES supports visual and high-dimensional vector inputs without image-specific augmentations.
method: Use an adversarial objective to make latent states sufficient for predicting rewards and next latent states.
Apply a fixed-capacity latent bottleneck to encourage removal of irrelevant variation.
Connect global optima to bisimulation on histories when exact sufficiency is attainable.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports state-of-the-art Distracting Control Suite performance, evaluations on Realistic ManiSkill and a 100-link swimmer, and latent-space probes supporting distractor invariance.
infographic.watch_item: The bisimulation guarantee assumes exact sufficiency is attainable; practical performance may depend on bottleneck capacity and adversarial optimization.
infographic.paper_title: Distractor-Robust Reinforcement Learning via Variational Bisimulation

title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
authors: Charlie Griffin, Oliver Makins, Asa Cooper Stickland, Alessandro Abate, Yarin Gal, Abby D'Cruz
abstract: AI monitors, classifiers that flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, are often evaluated against transcripts generated by attack policies acting as proxies for dangerous behaviour in deployment. We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study and find that measured false negative rate is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method. This rate ranged from 0.5\% to 20.8\% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4\% to 23.0\% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs.\ transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported results show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong. The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. The transcripts produced by attack policies are proxies for the dangerous behaviour a monitor must flag in deployment. These proxies can introduce visible artefacts, such as reasoning about a ``side task'' absent from the instructions shown to the monitor, that affect monitor judgements. Given the sensitivity above, the choice of proxy can change an evaluation's conclusion. Reading these results as evidence about deployment therefore requires a separate legitimacy argument for why the proxies are informative, including any justification of conservativeness. Making convincing arguments remains an open problem.

infographic.key_insight: Attack-policy selection can substantially change measured monitor evasion rates, making basic evaluations falsely reassuring.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Monitor evaluations should vary attack-generation methods and optimisation levels, and justify why simulated attacks represent deployment risks.
method: Evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor using attack-generated transcripts.
Develop attacks against proxy monitors and test transfer to a held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor.
Compare attack-generation methods and optimisation levels.
infographic.evidence_signal: Measured false negative rates ranged from 0.5% to 20.8% across reinforcement-learning optimisation levels and from 6.4% to 23.0% across methods at their best observed optimisation levels.
infographic.watch_item: Attack transcripts may contain artefacts that influence monitor judgments, so transfer success alone does not establish deployment relevance or conservativeness.
infographic.paper_title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators

title: Put the World Back: Timestamps Matter in Time Series Reasoning
authors: Tingrui Huang, Yuanyuan Deng, Qingren Yao, Joaquin Vanschoren, Mykola Pechenizkiy, Songgaojun Deng
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to time series reasoning. However, current evaluations often give models events in chronological order and already matched to the time series. This makes it unclear whether models use timestamps to connect events with observations or simply take shortcuts. To expose this ambiguity, we reformulate time series reasoning from a world-to-series projection perspective, viewing timestamps as explicit indices that connect numerical observations and external events to shared world states. We identify three structures that timestamps can make explicit: temporal causal structure, time semantics, and event-series alignment. Building on this perspective, we develop a diagnostic protocol that distinguishes timestamp-grounded reasoning from correlational shortcuts, a distinction that accuracy-based benchmarks cannot make. Controlled interventions on 310 questions from two tasks show that high accuracy can persist when timestamps are replaced by relative offsets or removed, while breaking event-series alignment induces systematic failures. When context is pre-aligned, models barely need timestamps. When order is missing, they use dates to recall world knowledge. Without dates, they rely on correlational shortcuts and rarely notice incorrect timestamps. These findings show that high accuracy on pre-aligned, ordered inputs does not establish that a model uses timestamps to synchronize observations with the world. We release our code, model outputs, and trajectory labels at https://github.com/tingrui-huang/timestamps-matter.

infographic.key_insight: High accuracy on pre-aligned, chronologically ordered time series tasks does not establish that LLMs use timestamps to connect observations with real-world events.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evaluate timestamp dependence and event-series alignment explicitly before trusting LLMs to synchronize numerical data with external events.
method: Model timestamps as shared indices linking numerical observations and external events to world states.
Distinguish temporal causal structure, time semantics, and event-series alignment.
Use controlled interventions to distinguish timestamp-grounded reasoning from correlational shortcuts.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 310 questions from two tasks, high accuracy could persist with relative offsets or no timestamps, while disrupted event-series alignment induced systematic failures.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence comes from two tasks; generalization to other time series domains and deployment settings remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Put the World Back: Timestamps Matter in Time Series Reasoning

title: Barron Smoothness for Layers in Deep Neural Networks
authors: G. Welper
abstract: In order to bound approximation errors for deep neural networks, we split the problem into two steps: First the selection of optimal infinite width limits for each layer and second an optimal discretization of all layers to obtain finite sized networks. We show that in expectation, the latter problem is equivalently characterized by a layer wise generalization of Barron norms. Moreover, we provide an analysis of the optimization landscape and show that local minima are characterized by an equidistribution principle akin to similar ideas in adaptive spline and finite element approximation.

infographic.key_insight: Layer-wise generalizations of Barron norms characterize expected optimal discretization errors when converting infinite-width layers into finite neural networks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The theory offers a framework for analyzing finite-network approximation error by separating layer selection from discretization.
method: Select optimal infinite-width limits for each layer.
Optimally discretize all layers into a finite network.
Analyze local minima through an equidistribution principle.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical characterizations of expected discretization error and local minima, but no datasets or empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish a practical algorithm for attaining the optimal discretizations.
infographic.paper_title: Barron Smoothness for Layers in Deep Neural Networks

title: Split-RL: Local Conflict Resolution in Reinforcement Learning
authors: Benjamin Fuhrer, Chen Tessler, Gal Dalal
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) policies are often trained by mixing contradictory feedback that is localized in space and time. For example, a robot may prioritize speed in open areas versus precision in tight gaps. We introduce Split-RL, a Gradient Boosting Trees (GBT) algorithm that uses guidance labels to locally isolate these conflicting signals. Standard neural networks (NNs) lack the structural mechanism to do this, as their parameters share feedback from all sources. While GBT provides the inductive bias to explicitly partition the state-space per objective, standard tree-fitting procedures aggregate contradictory gradient signals before they reach the leaves. Split-RL leverages this bias to integrate guidance labels into tree construction, routing these updates into disjoint state-space regions and preventing signal interference. Such labels can arise from heuristics, sensor-derived events, or existing rule-based systems, allowing Split-RL to incorporate rule-derived structure while retaining a learned policy. We theoretically show how early gradient aggregation loses objective-specific information and characterize when the Split-RL score isolates conflicting updates. We focus on constrained RL and offline RL with mixed datasets, each balancing two objectives that conflict locally. Across domains with spatial, rare-event, and temporal conflicts, Split-RL consistently outperforms existing methods by meeting the episodic cost budget while maintaining competitive rewards. In offline settings, Split-RL localizes the tradeoff between imitation and policy improvement, outperforming other methods and achieving near-expert performance across varying dataset sizes.

infographic.key_insight: Split-RL uses guidance labels to separate locally conflicting learning signals during tree construction, reducing interference between objectives.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a way to incorporate heuristic, sensor-derived, or rule-based guidance into learned policies that must balance reward, constraints, or imitation.
method: Build gradient-boosted tree policies with guidance-aware splits.
Route conflicting updates into disjoint state-space regions before gradient aggregation loses objective-specific information.
Apply local conflict resolution to constrained RL and offline learning from mixed datasets.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluations across spatial, rare-event, and temporal conflicts, with episodic cost-budget compliance and competitive rewards, plus near-expert offline performance across varying dataset sizes.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on informative guidance labels; the abstract does not quantify robustness to noisy or unavailable labels.
infographic.paper_title: Split-RL: Local Conflict Resolution in Reinforcement Learning

title: TASK Memory: Beyond Text-Only Memory with Activation Steering and Knowledge Editing against Memory Hallucination
authors: Jinkun Zhao, Wenjun Wu
abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on external memory, yet they still hallucinate about what they remember. Often the correct memory is retrieved and placed in the prompt, but the answer contradicts it or the memory is applied to the wrong question. We call these use-time memory hallucinations. Across five open models, we find that they arise from the conflict between parametric knowledge and external memory and take three forms: memory-ignoring, where the model returns to a stale fact in its weights (up to 46% of queries); memory-misapplying, where it attributes the memory to unrelated entities (up to 24%, and 49% when retrieval is combined with weight editing); and version confusion, where 53% of answers about revised facts assert the superseded value when both versions remain stored. We propose TASK memory, which goes beyond text-only memory by combining a Text note with Activation Steering and Knowledge editing that share one in-model address. The text holds the content. A removable knowledge edit supplies the address through its subject key and supports multi-hop composition. A pair of steering vectors decides, query by query, whether the model adopts the memory or keeps its own answer; the vectors store no content and control how the text memory is used. On frozen models under a pre-registered, test-once protocol, TASK reduces memory-ignoring hallucinations to at most 1.5% in all ten model-dataset cells and cuts neighbour misuse from 39.2% to 7.5% (+10.8 pp composite on CounterFact). It improves a 300-memory library over BM25 RAG by 16.4 pp, an advantage that holds at 3,000 memories, resolves fact revisions without fact IDs, and adds 7.5 pp of multi-hop accuracy on MQuAKE. 21 of 23 cross-model comparisons (8B-27B, four families) are significant, and TASK beats three recent context-steering methods in 9 of 10 model-dataset cells.

infographic.key_insight: TASK memory reduces hallucinations even when the correct memory is already retrieved by controlling whether an LLM applies external memory or relies on its parametric knowledge.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Memory-backed agents may need query-dependent control inside the model, not just better retrieval, to handle updated facts without misapplying them to unrelated entities.
method: Store factual content in an external text note.
Use a removable knowledge edit to provide a shared in-model address and support multi-hop composition.
Apply two content-free steering vectors to control memory adoption query by query.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five open models under a pre-registered, test-once protocol, TASK reduced memory-ignoring hallucinations to at most 1.5% in all ten model–dataset cells, with 21 of 23 cross-model comparisons statistically significant.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment requires internal activation access and removable weight edits; the abstract does not establish reliability beyond the tested 8B–27B open models and memory libraries of up to 3,000 entries.
infographic.paper_title: TASK Memory: Beyond Text-Only Memory with Activation Steering and Knowledge Editing against Memory Hallucination
